title: Syllabus
text:
Course Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Identify the role of statistics in criminology and criminal justice research.
Distinguish between different types of data and levels of measurement.
Import, clean, transform, and visualize real data in R using modern (tidyverse) tools.
Apply descriptive statistics to summarize and interpret data.
Explain the concepts of probability and distributions as they relate to criminological data.
Conduct and interpret basic statistical tests — from both frequentist and Bayesian perspectives — including t-tests, ANOVA, correlation, and regression.
Critically evaluate statistical claims in criminal justice policy and research.
Effectively communicate statistical findings in both written and visual formats.

Attendance is mandatory for our weekly class meetings. We all have busy lives, so while being on time is expected, I’d rather you miss ten minutes than a whole class. Students are expected to fully engage in class discussion and participate in the in-class exercises. The purpose of the class is for everyone to discuss the readings, not to have them explained.
I generally do not take formal attendance; however, during most weeks there is a graded in-class exercise. Points for these exercises are awarded based on active participation in class that day, and these points cannot be made up. Missing class means missing the opportunity to earn them.
Consider the following (simulated data, courtesy of an approach by Steven Miller): a simple linear regression of a student’s final grade on percentage of classes attended suggests an increase of one percent in attendance leads to an estimated increase of 0.704 in the final grade. One missed class is roughly a five-percent decrease in semester attendance — an estimated decrease of 3.52 in the overall grade. The effect is precise (t = 20.37) and the likelihood of no actual relationship is almost zero (R² = 0.342).

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
The Situation
Over three months, 40 bank robberies strike across a city’s five zones: North, South, East, West, and Downtown.

No clear pattern. No suspects. No leads.
The robber hits banks, disappears, and resurfaces days later in a different part of the city.
Detectives are stumped. The media is escalating. Public concern is growing.
Then someone makes a call to the PD’s new crime analyst team:



“Can you help us predict where they’ll hit next?”

How many robberies already happened in that zone?

title: Statistics is Awesome!

Before We Model, We Look
Very little information is available: no suspect descriptions, no MO patterns — just when and where.
Can we use this simple dataset to build a predictive model with statistics?

But before we even build a model, we can use basic plots to spot patterns.
Good data analysts always visualize before they model.

Building a Predictive Model
We want to predict where the next robbery will occur within a short time window, based on patterns in time, location, and prior activity.
Key predictors:

Day of year (captures seasonal or other unobserved time patterns)
Prior robberies in the same zone
Zone

title: Statistics is Awesome!
section: What Are We Trying to Predict?
text:
What Are We Trying to Predict?
We use logistic regression to predict whether the same zone will be hit again within 10 days:

Outcome: future_hit = 1 if another robbery occurs in the same zone within the next 10 days; otherwise 0
This creates a binary classification problem

(Don’t worry about the machinery today — logistic regression is Session 12. This is a preview of where we’re headed.)

Case Study Wrap-Up & Discussion
Outcome: Within days, officers apprehended the suspect in the predicted area as he was approaching a bank.
Statistics turned scattered crime data into a clear lead — saving time, resources, and preventing further victimization.

What data did we not use? How could we update this model as new robberies occur in real time?
What are the risks of over-relying on a model? How do we communicate uncertainty to decision-makers?
What other areas that interest you could statistics be applied to?

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Types of Data
Qualitative (categorical)

Describe groups or labels (zone, sex, race)
Text / interviews

Quantitative (numerical)

Measurable amounts (age, prior robberies)
Discrete = whole counts (number of robberies)
Continuous = can take any value (income, age)

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Levels of Measurement








Level
Definition
Examples




Nominal
Categories without order
Race, sex, zone


Ordinal
Ordered categories, unequal gaps
Likert scales


Interval
Meaningful differences, no true zero
Temperature (°C)


Ratio
Meaningful differences and true zero
Robbery counts, age

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Why Does the Level Matter?

Your variable’s scale determines the math you’re allowed to do
It also determines the plot you should make
Using the wrong scale leads to wrong conclusions

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Scale Determines the Math: Nominal

# WRONG: the "mean zone" is meaningless
rob$zone |> as.numeric() |> mean()

[1] 3.17




# RIGHT: counts and percentages
rob |>
  count(zone) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  zone         n   pct
  <fct>    <int> <dbl>
1 Downtown    32  16  
2 East        28  14  
3 North       59  29.5
4 South       36  18  
5 West        45  22.5

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Scale Determines the Math: Ordinal

# Summarize a Likert item (ordinal): median & IQR
rob |>
  summarize(med = median(risk_likert), iqr = IQR(risk_likert))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    med   iqr
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     4     3

# Association with a numeric variable: Spearman (rank-based)
cor(rob$risk_likert, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.001707403

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Interval vs. Ratio

mean(rob$temp_c)             # ~20 °C

[1] 20.07643

mean(rob$temp_c * 1.8 + 32)  # same temperatures in °F

[1] 68.13757


Temperature has no true zero — 0 °C is just where water freezes.

“30 °C is 10 °C warmer than 20 °C” ✔ (differences are fine)
“20 °C is twice as hot as 10 °C” ✘ (ratios are meaningless)



mean(rob$age)

[1] 40.605


Age has a true zero — a 40-year-old is twice as old as a 20-year-old. Differences and ratios both work.

title: Statistics is Awesome!
section: Choosing the Right Test (Preview of the Semester)
text:
Choosing the Right Test (Preview of the Semester)

# Categorical × categorical → chi-squared (compare proportions)
chisq.test(table(rob$zone, rob$caught))




    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table(rob$zone, rob$caught)
X-squared = 2.1521, df = 4, p-value = 0.7078



# Numeric by category → ANOVA (compare group means)  [Session 8]
aov(age ~ zone, data = rob) |> summary()



             Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
zone          4     73   18.15   0.134   0.97
Residuals   195  26419  135.48               



# Numeric × numeric → Pearson correlation             [Session 10]
cor(rob$age, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone)



[1] -0.004038644

title: Statistics is Awesome!
section: Treating Ordinal as Numeric Can Mislead
text:
Treating Ordinal as Numeric Can Mislead

educ <- rep(1:5, each = 50)                 # ordinal codes 1..5
income <- rep(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 1000), each = 50)  # HUGE jump at the top
cor(educ, income)                           # Pearson looks "strong"

[1] 0.7088768



The correlation is “large,” but the categories are not equally spaced — code numbers ≠ measurements.

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "swirl", "BayesFactor", "here"))




If RStudio won’t open, make sure R is installed first — RStudio requires it.
If you get a message about an outdated R version, install the newest R, then restart RStudio.

text:
Wednesdays, 5:50–8:35 pm · Currell 204 · Dr. Scott M. Mourtgos · mourtgos@mailbox.sc.edu

title: The Chicago Anchor Dataset
section: Important caveats — we will return to these all semester
text:
Important caveats — we will return to these all semester

Reported crime only. These data reflect crimes reported to and recorded by CPD — not all crime that occurred. Reporting rates differ across offense types and communities.
An arrest is not a conviction, and arrest_rate reflects incident clearance patterns, not “guilt rates.”
The ACS measures are survey estimates with sampling error, larger for smaller areas.
Aggregate (community-level) associations do not license conclusions about individuals — we’ll name this properly (the ecological fallacy) when we get to correlation.

title: The Chicago Anchor Dataset
text:
Provenance
Snapshot pulled July 2026; build script archived in the course repository (R/build-anchor-dataset.R) so the dataset is exactly reproducible. Sources: Chicago Data Portal, Crimes 2001–present (dataset ijzp-q8t2) and CMAP Community Data Snapshots 2026 (CCA table).

title: Homework 2 · Descriptive Statistics in R
text: Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answers to any interpretive questions. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.

title: Homework 2 · Descriptive Statistics in R
text:
Part 1: Measures of Central Tendency

Create a numeric vector with these sentence lengths (in years):
sentences <- c(2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 30)
Calculate the mean, median, and mode of these sentences. Use both the manual (hard-coded) method and the built-in functions: mean(), median(), and mfv() from the modeest package.
Plot a histogram of the sentence data. You may use ggplot() + geom_histogram() (as in Lab 2) or base R’s hist() — your choice.
Interpretation (in a comment): why might the mean give a misleading impression of typical sentence length in this example?

title: Homework 2 · Descriptive Statistics in R
text:
Part 2: Measures of Dispersion

Create two vote-count scenarios:
scenario1 <- c(175, 300, 425)
scenario2 <- c(299, 300, 301)
Compute the range of each using range() and diff().
Compute the deviations from the mean for each set (subtract the mean from each value).
Compute the sum of squared deviations, variance, and standard deviation — using:

the manual (hard-coded population) formulas, and
the built-in functions var() and sd().

(You’ll notice the built-ins give slightly different answers than your population formulas — R divides by n − 1. We’ll see exactly why in Session 4; for now, just note the difference in a comment.)
Compare the two vote scenarios: what do these measures tell you about the difference between the two vote distributions?

title: Homework 2 · Descriptive Statistics in R
text:
Part 3: Exploring Distributions

Generate and plot a normal distribution using a different mean and standard deviation than used in class, e.g.:
hist(rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 70, sd = 15))
Generate and plot a Poisson distribution with lambda = 1, and again with lambda = 5.
Reflection (in a comment):

What’s the key difference in shape between the normal and Poisson distributions?
Why might a Poisson distribution be useful in a criminal justice setting?

title: Homework 2 · Descriptive Statistics in R
text:
Part 4: Real Data (new this year)

Load the course anchor data:
library(tidyverse)
areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv")
Compute the mean, median, and standard deviation of violent_rate (violent crimes per 1,000 residents across Chicago’s 77 community areas).
Make a histogram of violent_rate.
Interpretation (in a comment): based on the mean-vs-median comparison and the histogram’s shape, is violent_rate symmetric or skewed? What does that tell you about how violence is distributed across Chicago’s communities?

title: Lab 2 · First Plots with ggplot2
text:
Walkthrough
A histogram — the shape of a numeric variable
Today’s lecture was about summarizing numeric variables. A histogram is the picture version:

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of incarcerated persons",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Count")







Anatomy of every ggplot: data (prisoners), aesthetics (aes(x = age) — which variables map to which visual channels), and geometry (geom_histogram() — how to draw them).
How does the picture relate to the numbers?

prisoners |>
  summarize(mean_age = mean(age), median_age = median(age), sd_age = sd(age))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_age median_age sd_age
     <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
1     34.5         34   10.2


A bar chart — counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = offense_type)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Offense types", x = NULL, y = "Count")







A boxplot — a distribution split by groups

The five-number-summary as a picture, one box per offense type:

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = offense_type, y = sentence_years)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  labs(title = "Sentence length by offense type",
       x = NULL, y = "Sentence (years)")







The box is the middle 50% (median = the line inside); the dots are outliers — the same “one 30-year sentence” problem from lecture, visible instantly.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
This Week
Topic: Descriptive statistics and statistical vocabulary

Measures of central tendency
Measures of dispersion
Distributions and their shapes

Learning goals: define in your own words — mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation, histogram, normal distribution, Poisson distribution — and use R to describe a small dataset and plot a distribution.
R4DS thread: you read Ch. 1 (Data visualization) & Ch. 2 (Workflow) — today’s lab puts both to work.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Three Ways to Say “Typical”



Measure
Meaning




Mean
the average


Median
the halfway point


Mode
the most frequently occurring value



Measures of central tendency summarize a vector of data by locating the typical, the middle, or the most common point.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Mean

rainfall <- c(0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 4)   # rain each day this week

# The hard way:
sum(rainfall) / length(rainfall)

[1] 1.142857




# The easy way:
mean(rainfall)

[1] 1.142857

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Median

rainfall

[1] 0 0 0 2 1 1 4

sort(rainfall)   # middle value of the sorted data?

[1] 0 0 0 1 1 2 4




median(rainfall)

[1] 1

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Mode

rainfall          # which value appears most often?

[1] 0 0 0 2 1 1 4

library(modeest)  # install.packages("modeest") once, library() every session
mfv(rainfall)     # mfv = "most frequent value"

[1] 0

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What Do These Look Like?

stats <- tibble(
  measure = c("Mean", "Median", "Mode"),
  value = c(mean(rainfall), median(rainfall), mfv(rainfall))
)
ggplot(tibble(rainfall), aes(rainfall)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(data = stats, aes(xintercept = value, color = measure),
             linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Rainfall with Mean, Median, and Mode",
       x = "Rainfall (inches)", y = "Frequency", color = NULL)

section: Why We Care in CJ: Sentencing

Why We Care in CJ: Sentencing

# Sentence lengths for 10 people convicted of robbery (years)
sentences <- c(2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 30)   # note the outlier!

mean(sentences)

[1] 6.1

median(sentences)

[1] 3.5

mfv(sentences)

One 30-year sentence drags the mean to 6.1 — nobody in the data actually got a “typical” 6-year sentence.

section: The Same Thing in Real Data
text:
The Same Thing in Real Data
Community-level crime rates in Chicago, 2025:

areas |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate   = mean(crime_rate),
    median_rate = median(crime_rate),
    max_rate    = max(crime_rate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_rate median_rate max_rate
      <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      96.9          82     292.




areas |> slice_max(crime_rate, n = 3) |> select(community, crime_rate)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  community          crime_rate
  <chr>                   <dbl>
1 Fuller Park              292.
2 West Garfield Park       220.
3 Englewood                214.


The Loop’s rate (driven by a small residential population and huge daytime crowds) pulls the mean above the median — same lesson as the 30-year sentence, in live data.

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: The Same Thing in Real Data
text: The Same Thing in Real Data

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Central Tendency Isn’t the Whole Story
text:
Central Tendency Isn’t the Whole Story
Three people run for city council; only the top two vote-getters win:


Scenario 1

A = 200 votes
B = 300 votes
C = 400 votes


Scenario 2

X = 299 votes
Y = 300 votes
Z = 301 votes


In both cases the average is 300. But scenario 1 has much greater spread in support; scenario 2 is tightly clustered — it’s hard to say who’s truly “preferred.”
→ We need measures of dispersion: range, deviations, variance, standard deviation.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Range

votes1 <- c(200, 300, 400)   # wide spread
votes2 <- c(299, 300, 301)   # tight cluster

mean(votes1); mean(votes2)   # identical means

[1] 300


[1] 300




range(votes1); diff(range(votes1))

[1] 200 400


[1] 200

range(votes2); diff(range(votes2))

[1] 299 301


[1] 2

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Deviations from the Mean

votes1 - mean(votes1)

[1] -100    0  100

votes2 - mean(votes2)

[1] -1  0  1



Why can’t we just sum the deviations?

sum(votes1 - mean(votes1))   # they always cancel to zero!

[1] 0

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Sum of Squares
Squaring makes every deviation positive (and emphasizes big misses):

sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2)

[1] 20000

sum((votes2 - mean(votes2))^2)

[1] 2

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Variance and SD

# Variance = mean squared deviation (population formula)
sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2) / length(votes1)

[1] 6666.667

# Standard deviation = square root of variance (back to vote units!)
sqrt(sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2) / length(votes1))

[1] 81.64966




var(votes1); sd(votes1)   # R's built-ins use the SAMPLE formula (divide by n-1)

[1] 10000


[1] 100

var(votes2); sd(votes2)   # more on WHY in Session 4

[1] 1


[1] 1

title: Descriptive Statistics
text: Seeing the Machinery

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Standard Deviation, in Words
The standard deviation measures how spread out the data are around the mean.

“On average, how far is each value from the mean?”

We square the deviations (to make them positive and emphasize larger differences), average them (that’s the variance), then take the square root (back to the original units).

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Why the Standard Deviation?

Same units as the data — variance is in squared units; SD is interpretable
Works with the normal distribution — SD tells us how typical or extreme a value is
The basis for many tools — confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, z-scores, regression all rely on it
Lets you compare variability across datasets with similar scales

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
In CJ Scenarios
Response times for patrol officers:

Low SD → officers respond in consistently similar times
High SD → sometimes fast, sometimes slow — inconsistency that matters for policy, supervision, training

Sentence lengths for the same crime:

High SD might suggest inconsistency — or bias — in sentencing

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Real Data: Consistency Across Communities

# Violent-crime rates: how much do Chicago communities differ?
areas |>
  summarize(
    mean_violent = mean(violent_rate),
    sd_violent   = sd(violent_rate),
    min_violent  = min(violent_rate),
    max_violent  = max(violent_rate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  mean_violent sd_violent min_violent max_violent
         <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1         30.7       22.5           4        111.


The SD is nearly as large as the mean — Chicago communities differ enormously in violence exposure. That inequality is a finding, and it took exactly one line of dispersion statistics to see it.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What Is a Distribution?
A distribution shows how many observations fall at different values — the shape of the data.
It answers:

“Where do most of the values fall?”
“How spread out are they?”
“Are some values rare or common?”

We visualize distributions with a histogram.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Normal Distribution

sims <- tibble(x = rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 100, sd = 10))
ggplot(sims, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey80", color = "white")


Symmetrical, bell-shaped; defined by two numbers — the mean (center) and SD (spread). Try different values!

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: SD and the Normal: the Empirical Rule
text:
SD and the Normal: the Empirical Rule


pct_within <- function(k) 100 * (pnorm(k) - pnorm(-k))
tibble(k = 1:3, pct_within = round(pct_within(1:3), 2))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
      k pct_within
  <int>      <dbl>
1     1       68.3
2     2       95.4
3     3       99.7

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Poisson Distribution

pois_sims <- tibble(x = rpois(n = 1000, lambda = 1))
ggplot(pois_sims, aes(x)) + geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["navy"])


Often skewed, especially when λ is low. Models counts of rare events: 911 calls per hour, crimes per day, cars per minute. One parameter: λ = expected number of events. Try different values!

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Poisson Is Not Hypothetical
Daily robbery counts in our Chicago sample, all of 2025:

daily_robberies <- crimes |>
  filter(primary_type == "ROBBERY") |>
  count(date)

ggplot(daily_robberies, aes(n)) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  labs(x = "Robberies per day", y = "Number of days",
       title = "Real crime counts look Poisson")

title: Descriptive Statistics

Why We Care About Distributions in CJ

The normal distribution helps us understand common variation (response times, test scores)
The Poisson distribution models event counts, especially rare ones — crimes, incidents — and underlies many forecasting tools
Recognizing the shape of your data is the first step in choosing the right analysis — a theme for the whole semester
